newsitem.title: BOSNIA: FEATURE - Franciscans in Bosnia rebel against Vatican.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Franciscans in Bosnia rebel against Vatican.

text.p: Only days before Pope John Paul II pays an historic visit to the Bosnian capital Sarajevo, brotherly love is in short supply among the country's feuding Catholic clergy.
"It's sad. This dispute is creating a division among the faithful," said Tomislav Pervan, Franciscan provincial for the western Herzegovina region.
Pervan and his fellow Franciscans are locked in a bitter dispute with diocesan clergy over who will wield authority in Herzegovina, home of the country's largest Catholic Croat community.

The Franciscans, who first arrived in Bosnia 700 years ago to spread the Catholic faith, have refused to give up control of parishes in Herzegovina and continued to administer to their flock in defiance of the Vatican.
The Franciscans say they are asking only to preserve their traditional role in Herzegovina.
The Vatican and the local bishop say the Franciscans have to obey the church's hierarchy and ordered them to stop promoting the town of Medjugorje as a pilgrimage site.
Despite the Vatican's disapproval, thousands of Christians travel to the western town of Medjugorje every year to hear Franciscans speak of an alleged apparition of the Virgin Mary.
Croatian journalists say the Herzegovina dispute grows out of a struggle for power and control of church finances, not a debate about religious dogma.
"It's about authority and funds, because Medjugorje is a profitable place," said one journalist in Zagreb, who asked not to be named.
"The church has no political influence over Herzegovina people but Franciscans carry a lot of weight."
Both the diocese and the Franciscans deny money plays any role in their quarrel.
ROW CAME TO A HEAD LAST YEAR
The power struggle came to a head last May, when Rome ordered Franciscan priests in the town of Capljina to allow the diocese to take over the parish church.
The Franciscans did not leave and when priests appointed by the diocese arrived in Capljina, an angry crowd surrounded their cars and prevented them from entering the church car park.
"The priests had reasonable fears they would be physically attacked," said Zeljko Majic, a priest in the Herzegovina diocese.
Supporters of the Franciscans have blocked the doorway of the Capljina church with concrete blocks and posted banners in four languages vowing to keep the diocesan priests away.
The Franciscans' stubborn refusal to obey the Vatican mirrors the hard-headed reputation of Herzegovina, known for its severe landscape and hardline Croat nationalists.
The Vatican has had to tread carefully in Herzegovina because the Franciscans enjoy a popular following and strong ties with wealthy emigres and the ruling Croat nationalist party.
After 10 rounds of talks in the Vatican, Pervan said he believes his Franciscan priests must drop their protests and submit to the will of the church.
"We must obey, we must make peace. That is the only way out," Pervan said.
Although he said he has ordered his priests to withdraw from Capljina and other churches, local residents say the Franciscan priests still perform their duties in secret.
The diocese says any clandestine baptisms, weddings and confessions conducted by the Franciscans are illegal as far as the Vatican is concerned.
If the Franciscan rebels persist, the church could be forced to excommunicate them, Majic said.
"I think we can say that the Vatican is seriously considering this (excommunication). The Vatican has already set some deadlines," he said.
HARDER JOB TO BRING ABOUT CROAT/MOSLEM RECONCILIATION

Even if Rome succeeds in scaling back the role of the Franciscans in the region, it faces a much tougher task in convincing Herzegovina Croats to embrace Papal appeals for reconciliation with their wartime Moslem foes, analysts say.

Church officials fear that many Croats from Herzegovina, who fought a 10-month war against Moslems in 1993-94, may choose not to travel to Sarajevo to hear the Pope speak about Bosnian statehood in a city which now has a Moslem majority.
By declining invitations to visit Herzegovina during his trip to Bosnia, the Pope has sent a clear message to the Franciscans.
"I think he knows about the whole affair," said Pervan. "And his opinion is we have to obey."
